content: Posterior blepharitis is a prevalent condition that leads to damage of the ocular surface and eyelids, as well as significant discomfort. It affects approximately 37% to 47% of ophthalmology patients, with its incidence increasing with age. This condition is multifactorial in nature and is often associated with other pathologies, including rosacea, meibomianitis, and infections. Standard treatment strategies typically aim to alleviate symptoms through the use of artificial tears, lid scrubs, and warm compresses. However, managing chronic blepharitis effectively can be particularly challenging. One potential therapeutic approach involves the use of oral antibiotics, which possess both antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties. Despite this, there are currently no established guidelines regarding the type of antibiotic, dosage, or duration of treatment for chronic blepharitis. The objective of this review was to evaluate the potential benefits and harms of oral antibiotics in individuals with chronic blepharitis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PubMed, LILACS, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, was conducted. No restrictions were applied regarding the date or language of the studies. The last search was performed on August 29, 2020. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared oral antibiotics with placebo in adult participants diagnosed with chronic blepharitis, including subtypes such as staphylococcal, seborrheic, or Meibomian Gland Dysfunction (MGD). Standard Cochrane methodology was employed, and the certainty of the evidence for six outcomes was assessed using the GRADE classification. Two studies involving a total of 220 participants were included in the review. The first study, a parallel-group RCT conducted in the United States, compared oral doxycycline (40 mg once daily) with placebo in 70 participants with blepharitis and facial rosacea. The follow-up period was three months. The second study, a three-arm RCT conducted in South Korea, evaluated the effects of high-dose (200 mg twice daily) and low-dose (20 mg twice daily) doxycycline versus placebo over a one-month treatment period. This study enrolled 150 participants with chronic MGD, with 50 participants in each study arm. The two studies assessed different outcome measures, precluding the possibility of a meta-analysis. The evidence regarding the effect of oral antibiotics on subjective symptom improvement was highly uncertain. In the first study, oral doxycycline appeared to have little to no effect on subjective symptoms, as measured by the Ocular Surface Disease Index (OSDI) scores (mean difference [MD] 3.55, 95% confidence interval [CI] −4.61 to 11.71; n = 70) and bulbar conjunctival hyperemia scores (MD −0.01, 95% CI −0.38 to 0.36; n = 70) at 12 weeks. In the second study, oral doxycycline may have slightly improved the number of symptoms (MD −0.56, 95% CI −0.95 to −0.17; n = 93 for high-dose doxycycline versus placebo; MD −0.48, 95% CI −0.86 to −0.10; n = 93 for low-dose doxycycline versus placebo) and the proportion of participants reporting symptom improvement (risk ratio [RR] 6.13, 95% CI 2.61 to 14.42; n = 93 for high-dose doxycycline versus placebo; RR 6.54, 95% CI 2.79 to 15.30; n = 93 for low-dose doxycycline versus placebo) at one month. However, the certainty of this evidence was judged to be very low. One study assessed aqueous tear production using Schirmer's test (measured in mm/5 minutes, with higher scores indicating better tear production) and tear film stability using tear film break-up time (TBUT, measured in seconds, with higher scores indicating better stability) at one month. The evidence, which was of very low certainty, suggested that oral doxycycline may improve these clinical signs. The estimated MD in Schirmer's test scores was 4.09 mm (95% CI 2.38 to 5.80; n = 93) for the high-dose doxycycline group compared to placebo and 3.76 mm (95% CI 1.85 to 5.67; n = 93) for the low-dose doxycycline group compared to placebo. The estimated MD in TBUT was 1.58 seconds (95% CI 0.57 to 2.59; n = 93) for the high-dose doxycycline group compared to placebo and 1.70 seconds (95% CI 0.96 to 2.44; n = 93) for the low-dose doxycycline group compared to placebo. While these findings indicate some improvement, the clinical significance of these changes remains uncertain. Adverse events were also reported. One study suggested that oral doxycycline may increase the risk of serious side effects. In the high-dose doxycycline group, 18 participants (39%) experienced serious adverse events, compared to 8 participants (17%) in the low-dose doxycycline group and 3 participants (6%) in the placebo group (RR 6.13, 95% CI 1.94 to 19.41; n = 93 for high-dose doxycycline versus placebo; RR 2.72, 95% CI 0.77 to 9.64; n = 93 for low-dose doxycycline versus placebo). Additionally, one study reported one case of migraine headache and five cases of headache in the oral doxycycline group, as well as one case of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma in the placebo group. The certainty of the evidence for adverse events was judged to be very low. In conclusion, the available evidence is insufficient to draw definitive conclusions regarding the use of oral antibiotics for chronic blepharitis. Very low-certainty evidence suggests that oral antibiotics may improve certain clinical signs but may also increase the risk of adverse events. The evidence for their effect on subjective symptom improvement is highly uncertain. Further high-quality trials are needed to provide more robust evidence on the efficacy and safety of oral antibiotics in the treatment of chronic blepharitis.
